strengths: Strong and comprehensive empirical results on challenging benchmarks: 1.8× median improvement in returns, 36% success rate improvement, with particularly impressive gains on long-horizon manipulation tasks (20× on jaco)
Thorough experimental evaluation across 40 tasks with diverse baselines (8 methods covering different paradigms), extensive ablations isolating each component, and convergence speed analysis

Clear problem motivation and well-articulated approach: clearly explains limitations of current RL pre-training methods and presents a principled solution combining latent intentions with flow occupancy models
Strong reproducibility: promised open-source implementation, detailed hyperparameters (Tables 1-3), comprehensive appendices, and clear algorithmic descriptions (Algorithms 1-2)
Principled theoretical grounding: ELBO formulation with information bottleneck connection (Appendix B.1) and justification for implicit GPI (Appendix B.2)
Effective ablation studies clearly demonstrate independent contributions of intention encoding (Fig. 4) and implicit GPI (Fig. 5) to overall performance
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: combines existing techniques (VAE-style intention inference, flow matching from [29], GPI from [9]) with paper acknowledging FB + FOM is equivalent to [29]. Primary contribution is combination rather than fundamental innovation

Consistency Assumption 1 is strong and empirically unvalidated: assumes consecutive transitions share same intention without validating this holds in actual datasets or analyzing failure modes when assumption is violated

Insufficient comparison to closely related work [29]: FB + FOM comparison limited to Fig. 4 with overlapping error bars and no deep analysis of why latent variable approach should dominate forward-backward representations

Significant hyperparameter sensitivity requiring domain-specific tuning: λ and α coefficients must be tuned per domain (Table 3, Fig. 7e-7f), with no domain-agnostic strategy proposed. This creates unfair advantage over baselines and raises practical deployment concerns

Evaluation methodology concerns: InFOM receives domain-specific hyperparameter tuning while baselines use uniform parameters; image-based evaluation uses only 4 seeds; some baselines excluded from image tasks; several OGBench tasks extremely sparse making conclusions difficult

Missing analysis of learned intentions: no visualization/interpretation of latent intention space, claims about 'simple and performant' inference weakly supported, no evaluation of occupancy model quality (only indirect downstream task performance)

Insufficient justification for SARSA over Q-learning TD flows: vague explanation of stability and 'counterfactual error avoidance' without direct empirical comparison showing SARSA outperforms Q-learning variant

Method complexity without computational analysis: multiple components (encoder, vector field, reward predictor, critic, policy) with combined losses, but no analysis of computational overhead relative to baselines despite longer training times (4-12 hours)

strengths: Comprehensive experimental evaluation on 40 diverse tasks with 8 baselines and thorough ablations
Strong empirical results on challenging manipulation tasks (20× improvement on Jaco)
Clear problem motivation and well-structured presentation with good reproducibility details
Faster policy learning during fine-tuning demonstrates practical benefits
Detailed hyperparameter studies and extensive appendix with implementation details
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: primarily combines existing ideas (amortized VAE inference + Farebrother et al.'s flow matching + expectile loss). Main contributions are incremental over [29]
Weak justification for intention conditioning: Fig 4 shows only marginal improvements over FB+FOM (the most similar baseline, equivalent to TD flows [29]) on 3/4 tasks, contradicting central claims
Problematic Assumption 1 (consecutive transitions share intentions) is strong and empirically unvalidated. No analysis of when this holds or robustness to violations

Questionable experimental fairness: InFOM's behavioral cloning coefficient α varies 3000× (0.1-300) across domains; unclear if baselines received equal tuning effort; DINO severely underperforms suggesting implementation issues

Missing critical ablations: no separate evaluation of intention conditioning vs. flow matching contributions; no analysis of when/why intention conditioning helps (large on Jaco, minimal on locomotion)
Implicit GPI not well justified: connection between 'avoiding ODE backprop' and 'expectile loss' unclear in main text; only 2-task validation in Fig 5; alternative approaches unexplored
Marginal improvements on easier tasks and inconsistent performance undermine generality claims
High hyperparameter sensitivity (Figs 7e-7f), especially to λ and α, requiring domain-specific tuning limits practical applicability

strengths: Comprehensive experimental evaluation: 40 tasks with 8 diverse baselines across multiple pre-training paradigms (behavioral cloning, representations, model-based, occupancy models, skill discovery), representing significantly above-average experimental rigor
Convincing results on hard tasks: 20× improvement on jaco and 36% success rate gain on OGBench demonstrate substantial practical impact; method handles tasks where baselines fail entirely

Thorough ablation studies: Validates intention encoding (5.2), implicit GPI benefits (5.3, showing 44% improvement with 8× lower variance), convergence properties (5.4), and extensive hyperparameter sensitivity (Appendix D)
Technical soundness: Correct ELBO derivation with insightful information bottleneck connection; well-motivated use of SARSA flows; principled implicit GPI design using expectile loss
Strong reproducibility: Detailed hyperparameters, implementation details, multiple random seeds (8 state-based, 4 image-based), and promised open-source code
Clear presentation: Well-motivated introduction establishing why time and intention reasoning matter in RL; effective use of figures; mathematically rigorous exposition
weaknesses: Limited conceptual novelty over Farebrother et al. [29]: Main differences are (i) variational intention encoder vs. forward-backward representations, (ii) expectile GPI vs. standard GPI. Section 5.2 shows InFOM outperforms FB on only 3/4 tasks, suggesting marginal advantage

Inconsistent improvements across domains: Large gains only on hard tasks (jaco, OGBench); similar performance to baselines on easier domains (cheetah, walker). Raises question whether improvements come from novel design or specialized inductive bias for complex exploration

Strong assumptions with limited validation: (i) Consistency Assumption assumes no task interleaving, not empirically tested; (ii) Intent inference from (s',a') is indirect—trajectory-level encoding not ablated; (iii) Trajectory reduction acknowledged as limitation but not investigated

Substantial hyperparameter sensitivity: λ and α require domain-specific tuning (Table 3 shows completely different values across domains); Fig. 7e,f show 100× performance swings with α. Contradicts foundation model philosophy; cost of hyperparameter search not discussed

Limited analysis of learned representations: No visualization/interpretation of learned intention distributions; unclear what z encodes (tasks? behaviors? rewards?); Section 5.2 shows intentions can be inferred but not what they capture; missing cluster analysis or semantic interpretation

Implicit GPI justification incomplete: Expectile loss chosen without comparing against alternatives (gradient clipping, other sampling strategies); Appendix B.2 provides intuition but lacks formal convergence guarantees; Fig. 5 compares only M=32 sampling variant

Incomplete comparison with most relevant baseline: FB + FOM (equivalent to TD flows + GPI) compared only on 4 tasks in Section 5.2; crucial for validating novelty over Farebrother et al., deserves full 40-task comparison

Image-based evaluation limited: Only 4 tasks with per-task hyperparameter tuning (vs. per-domain for state-based); unclear if 31% improvement generalizes or reflects evaluation setup; sample size too small for visual generalization claims

Missing computational cost analysis: Flow matching with T=10 steps + N=16 future states could be expensive; no wall-clock time comparisons; memory requirements unreported; pre-training compute (1M steps) not analyzed

Incomplete ablations: Policy fixed to Gaussian MLP (diffusion/flow policies not explored); N=16 future states appears fixed without justification; SARSA vs. Q-learning flows compared only theoretically, not empirically

strengths: Well-motivated problem: Clear identification that heterogeneous datasets benefit from intention modeling; relevant for practical pre-training scenarios
Comprehensive experimental evaluation: 40 tasks, 8 diverse baselines, extensive ablations, and hyperparameter analysis across domains
Thorough reproducibility: Detailed hyperparameters per domain, algorithm pseudocode, implementation details, and promised open-source code
Strong methodological rigor: Good ablation studies (implicit GPI, intention encoding mechanisms, behavioral cloning) with clear evidence of component importance
Solid technical integration: Coherent combination of flow matching, VAE inference, occupancy models, and policy extraction
Real-world validation: Evaluation on robotics dataset with learned embeddings
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: Incremental over Farebrother et al. (2025); main addition is straightforward VAE-based intention conditioning; expectile loss already used in offline RL

Inconsistent improvements: Large variance across tasks; simple domains show no improvement; dramatic gains only on hard manipulation tasks; 1.8× median driven by outliers (jaco 20×), not representative of typical tasks
Restrictive Assumption 1 (Consistency): Consecutive transitions sharing intention is strong; real users switch intentions mid-episode; assumption not empirically validated for robustness

Hyperparameter sensitivity and complexity: Critical hyperparameters (d, λ, α, µ) require extensive domain-specific tuning; same domain sometimes needs different values per task; Figure 15 shows large performance swings
Insufficient analysis of most related work: Limited comparison to Farebrother et al. (2025) / TD flows; Figure 8 shows comparable performance; unclear why complexity is justified
Weak intention analysis: Limited to 2 tasks; no systematic validation that intentions capture meaningful task structure; missing failed-case analysis
Implicit GPI approximation gap: Convergence requires N→∞, µ→1; practice uses N=16, µ≤0.99; no empirical analysis of distance from optimal policy
Limited novelty of components: VAE inference, expectile loss, flow matching are all standard; main contribution is their combination

strengths: Comprehensive experimental evaluation across 40 tasks with 8 diverse baselines and extensive ablations
Clear problem formulation addressing multi-user heterogeneous RL data collection
Technically sound combination of VAE inference with flow-matching occupancy models
Good empirical results on challenging manipulation tasks (36% success rate improvement) with visualizations showing learned intentions align with ground truth
Honest presentation including limitations and hyperparameter sensitivity analysis
Thorough reproducibility details with promised open-source implementation
weaknesses: Limited conceptual novelty: primarily combines existing techniques (VAE, occupancy measures, flow matching, TD flows); unclear what the meaningful difference is from Farebrother et al. (2025) beyond adding an intention encoder
Marginal improvements over closest prior (FB + FOM); many performance differences fall within error margins and InFOM doesn't consistently outperform alternative intention encoding schemes (Fig. 8)

Domain-dependent results: large improvements only on hardest tasks where all baselines collapse; on easier tasks performance is comparable; Fig. 10 shows 3.6× performance gap disappears with dense rewards, suggesting the improvement comes from reward structure rather than algorithmic superiority
Restrictive consistency assumption (Assumption 1) that consecutive transitions share intention—violated by skill switching and never empirically validated for robustness
Extensive hyperparameter tuning required (α ranges 3000×, λ 0.005-0.2, d 128-512) with clear sensitivity shown in Fig. 15; raises fairness of comparisons and generalization concerns
Weak theoretical justification: implicit GPI lacks rigorous justification beyond avoiding ODE backprop; information bottleneck connection (C.1) is underdeveloped and doesn't drive design decisions
Overstated sample efficiency claims: uses 5.5M total samples (5M pre-training + 500K fine-tuning) which is not particularly data efficient; no data-limited regime explored
Limited real-world validation: single robotics task using pre-trained encoder rather than end-to-end; insufficient evidence for deployment
Missing key ablations: no robustness test for consistency assumption violation; no comparison of intention encoding methods within same framework; limited failure case analysis

Statistical concerns: no significance tests despite overlapping error bars; improvements from near-zero baselines on some tasks are less meaningful; MC Q-estimation with N=16 introduces variance, yet requires behavioral cloning regularization to stabilize

strengths: Comprehensive experimental evaluation across 40 diverse tasks with strong baselines, demonstrating 1.8× median return improvement and 36% success rate improvement
Sensible technical approach combining variational intention inference with flow matching for occupancy modeling, well-grounded in theory with ELBO derivation and GPI analysis
Excellent reproducibility: open-source code, detailed hyperparameters for all methods, clear algorithms, and reasonable computational requirements (4-12 hours on single GPU)
Effective demonstration of interpretable intention learning (Figure 4) validated against prior intention encoding mechanisms, showing the method discovers meaningful behavioral clusters
Extensive ablations studying policy extraction strategies, intention encoding mechanisms, convergence speed, dataset sensitivity, and hyperparameter effects
Strong empirical performance across 6 of 8 domains with consistent improvements, including validation on real robotics datasets (Appendix F.1)
weaknesses: Limited novelty over most related work (Farebrother et al., 2025), which also uses flow matching for occupancy models; Figure 8 shows InFOM outperforms prior intention methods on only 3/4 tasks with modest margins

Sparse reward improvements are partially confounded by problem structure: dramatic 20× improvement on Jaco tasks explained by reward sparsity, with gap shrinking to 3.6× with dense rewards (Appendix F.4)

Significant hyperparameter sensitivity with behavioral cloning coefficient α varying across domains by a factor of 3000 (0.1-300), and latent dimension d requiring domain-specific tuning; large variance on some tasks (e.g., walker walk 467.3±82.1)

Consistency assumption (Assumption 1) that consecutive transitions share intentions is reasonable but impact not thoroughly investigated; acknowledged limitation about trajectory-to-transition reduction not always capturing original intentions
High data requirement (1M unlabeled transitions for good performance, Appendix F.6) may limit practical applicability; this data efficiency limitation not prominently discussed
Insufficient analysis of failure modes and when intention conditioning helps vs. hurts; unclear which components (encoder, SARSA flows, expectile distillation) are essential vs. auxiliary
